notes.h: Empirical and molecular formulae: the definitions
notes.b: A formula can tell you two different things about a compound: the simplest ratio of its atoms, or the exact number of atoms in one molecule. Keeping the two apart is the key to every formula calculation that follows.
points: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound, e.g. CH₂O, which says only that there are two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom for every carbon atom.
The molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule (a group of atoms bonded together), e.g. C₆H₁₂O₆ for glucose.
The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so C₆H₁₂O₆ is six times CH₂O.

For ionic compounds (compounds built from a lattice of positive and negative ions, not separate molecules) the formula is always the empirical formula, e.g. NaCl and MgO, because the formula only gives the simplest ratio of ions.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate an empirical formula from percentage composition and then find the molecular formula from Mr, so be clear which of the two you are being asked for.

notes.b: Percentage composition tells you what fraction of a compound's mass is made up by one element, or by one part such as water. It uses the relative atomic mass (Ar, the mass of an atom of the element compared with other atoms) and the relative molecular mass (Mr, the sum of the Ar values of all the atoms in the formula).
points: Relative atomic masses used in these calculations: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Mg 24, S 32, Cu 63.5.
Percentage by mass of an element = (number of atoms of the element × Ar ÷ Mr) × 100. You multiply Ar by the number of atoms because each atom in the formula contributes its mass.
Example: nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (Mr = 80): (2 × 14 ÷ 80) × 100 = 35.0%.
Example: water in hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·5H₂O (Mr = 249.5): (5 × 18 ÷ 249.5) × 100 = 36.1%. Here the 5 water molecules are treated as one part, each with a mass of 18.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate the percentage composition of an element in a compound. Write out the formula (number of atoms × Ar ÷ Mr) × 100 first, then substitute.

notes.b: Experiments measure masses or percentages, not atoms, so to get a formula you convert each element to moles (the chemist's counting unit, which lets you compare numbers of atoms) and then find the simplest ratio.
points: 1. Write the mass (or percentage) of each element.
2. Divide each by its relative atomic mass to get the number of moles, which turns masses into amounts that can be compared atom for atom.
3. Divide each by the smallest number of moles to get the ratio, so that the element present in the smallest amount becomes 1.
4. If the ratio is not whole (e.g. 1.5 or 1.33), multiply all values by 2 or 3 to get whole numbers.
Do not round a ratio such as 1.5 to 2; multiply all the values up instead, because rounding changes the ratio of atoms and gives the wrong formula.
Dividing by the smallest value, 3.33, gives H 6.7 ÷ 3.33 = 2.0, so the ratio is 1 : 2 : 1 and the empirical formula is CH₂O.
notes.tip: Don't round ratios such as 1.5 to 2; multiply up instead. Exams ask you to calculate an empirical formula from percentage composition.

notes.b: When a reaction gives the masses of the elements rather than percentages, the method is the same. Sometimes one mass has to be found by subtraction first, as in this example of magnesium burning in oxygen to form magnesium oxide.
points: Example from masses (sample data): 2.40 g of magnesium burns to give 4.00 g of magnesium oxide.
The mass of oxygen is the mass of oxide minus the mass of metal: 4.00 − 2.40 = 1.60 g, because the extra mass is the oxygen that combined with the magnesium.
Mg 2.40 ÷ 24 = 0.100 mol and O 1.60 ÷ 16 = 0.100 mol, so equal numbers of moles of each element combined.
The ratio Mg : O is 1 : 1, so the formula is MgO.
notes.tip: Mass of oxygen = mass of oxide − mass of metal. Don't use the mass of the oxide as the mass of oxygen.

notes.b: The empirical formula gives only the simplest ratio. If you also know the relative molecular mass (Mr), you can work out how many empirical units are in one real molecule.
points: 1. Divide the relative molecular mass (Mr) by the mass of the empirical formula unit (the sum of the Ar values in the empirical formula).
2. Multiply every number in the empirical formula by that result.
Example: empirical formula CH₂O (mass 30) and Mr = 180: 180 ÷ 30 = 6, so the molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆.
Example: a hydrocarbon (a compound of only carbon and hydrogen) of 85.7% C and 14.3% H, with Mr 56: C 85.7 ÷ 12 = 7.14 and H 14.3 ÷ 1 = 14.3.
Dividing by 7.14 gives the ratio 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (mass 14).
56 ÷ 14 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to find the molecular formula from Mr after finding the empirical formula, so keep the two answers labelled separately.

notes.b: You can find the formula of magnesium oxide by burning a known mass of magnesium and weighing the product. The gain in mass is the oxygen that combined, which gives the mole ratio.
points: 1. Weigh a clean crucible (a small heat-proof dish) and lid, add a coiled length of clean magnesium ribbon and reweigh.
2. Heat strongly, lifting the lid slightly from time to time to let air in (magnesium needs oxygen to burn) while keeping white smoke (magnesium oxide) from escaping.
3. When the magnesium no longer glows, remove the lid and heat strongly for a few more minutes.
4. Cool and reweigh, then heat, cool and reweigh again until the mass is constant (it stops changing, which shows the reaction is complete).
5. Calculate the masses of magnesium and of oxygen that combined, then their moles and ratio, as in the mass example for empirical formulae.
Safety: do not look directly at burning magnesium, which is very bright; the crucible is very hot, so use tongs and a heat-proof mat.

Diagram: a crucible with its lid on a pipeclay triangle (a wire frame with clay-covered sides that holds the crucible), on a tripod over a Bunsen burner; label the crucible, lid, pipeclay triangle, tripod and Bunsen burner.
notes.tip: Mass of oxygen = mass of oxide − mass of metal, so you only need the weighings before and after heating.

notes.b: Some salts hold water inside their crystals. This water is part of the formula, and heating a sample and measuring the mass lost lets you find how many water molecules there are for each unit of the salt.
points: Water of crystallisation is water chemically held in a fixed ratio within the crystals of some salts, shown after a dot in the formula, e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O and Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
Heating to constant mass drives off the water of crystallisation; for example, blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate turns white, becoming anhydrous (without water).
Example (sample data): 2.50 g of CuSO₄·xH₂O gives 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ (Mr 159.5) when heated to constant mass.
Mass of water lost: 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g, because the water is the only thing driven off on heating.
Moles of water: 0.90 ÷ 18 = 0.050 mol (Mr of H₂O = 18).
Moles of CuSO₄: 1.60 ÷ 159.5 = 0.0100 mol.
Ratio of water to CuSO₄ = 0.050 : 0.0100 = 5 : 1, so x = 5 and the formula is CuSO₄·5H₂O.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to find x in a hydrated salt from heating data. The water lost is the starting mass minus the final mass.

notes.b: A chemical equation is a short way of describing a reaction. It must follow the law of conservation of mass: atoms are neither made nor destroyed, so the equation has to balance.
points: A chemical equation shows the reactants (the substances that react, on the left) and the products (the substances formed, on the right), written as formulae.
A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, because atoms are conserved (law of conservation of mass).
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous, meaning dissolved in water.
The coefficients, the large numbers in front of formulae, give the ratio of moles, or molecules, that react.
For example, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means 2 mol of hydrogen react with 1 mol of oxygen to give 2 mol of water.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why an equation must be balanced and what the coefficients tell you. Give the conservation of atoms for the first and the ratio of moles for the second.

notes.b: Balancing is done by trial and adjustment, but following the same four steps each time keeps it reliable. The only things you may change are the coefficients.
points: 1. Write the correct formula of every reactant and product.
Never change a formula (the small subscript numbers) to balance an equation; change only the coefficients, because changing a subscript makes a different substance.
2. Count the atoms of each element on each side, so you can see which elements are unbalanced.
3. Balance by putting coefficients in front of formulae, starting with an element that appears in only one substance on each side.
Leave hydrogen, oxygen and any element on its own until last, because changing their coefficients disturbs the other elements least at that point.
4. Check every element again and make sure the coefficients are the smallest whole numbers.
Add state symbols to every formula, so the equation shows whether each substance is a solid, liquid, gas or in solution.
Hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are diatomic (their molecules have two atoms) and are written as H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.
notes.tip: Never change subscripts in a formula to balance; change only coefficients. Remember the diatomic elements H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. Exams ask you to write a balanced equation from a word description.

notes.b: Combustion means burning in oxygen. These four equations show how to balance a metal and three fuels, including one that needs a fraction doubled.
points: Magnesium burning: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
Methane burning: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
Propane burning: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l).
Ethane burning, with the fractional coefficient 3½ for O₂ doubled to give whole numbers: 2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to balance combustion equations. If you end up with a fraction, multiply every coefficient to clear it.

notes.b: These equations show a metal reacting with an acid, neutralisation (an acid reacting with a base), decomposition (one substance breaking down) and a metal reacting with water.
points: Aluminium and hydrochloric acid (metal and acid): 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g).
Neutralisation: 2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).
Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g).
Calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Sodium and water: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to balance equations of these types: neutralisation, metal and acid, and decomposition.

notes.b: In a solution, ionic compounds are split into separate ions. An ionic equation leaves out the ions that do nothing, so it shows only what really changes.
points: An ionic equation shows only the ions that take part in the reaction, leaving out spectator ions (ions that are unchanged in solution).
Example: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) becomes Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
In that reaction Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions, because they are in solution before and after the reaction.
Neutralisation of any strong acid by a strong base is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), because only the hydrogen and hydroxide ions react.
An ionic equation must balance in charge as well as in atoms, because charge is also conserved, e.g. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ cancel to give neutral AgCl.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to write an ionic equation. Remove the spectator ions and check that both atoms and charge balance.

notes.b: The coefficients in a balanced equation are mole ratios, so the equation tells you how much of one substance reacts with or makes another.
points: The balanced equation gives the mole ratio of any two substances in the reaction.
In propane burning, 1 mol of propane needs 5 mol of oxygen and produces 3 mol of carbon dioxide.
This mole ratio is the starting point for calculating masses of reactants and products. There is more on this in the chapter Stoichiometry: Limiting Reactants and Percentage Yield.

keyTerms.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.
The average mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a formula.
The amount of a substance whose mass in grams equals its relative atomic or molecular mass.
The percentage by mass of each element in a compound.
Water held in a fixed ratio within the crystals of some salts, shown after a dot in the formula.
Describes a salt with no water of crystallisation.
An equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
The large number written in front of a formula that gives the number of moles or molecules in the equation.
A symbol in brackets after a formula, (s), (l), (g) or (aq), showing its physical state.
An element whose molecules contain two atoms, such as O₂.
An equation showing only the ions that take part in a reaction.
An ion that is unchanged in solution and is left out of an ionic equation.
The ratio of the moles of two substances, given by the coefficients in a balanced equation.

questions.prompt: A compound contains 52.2% carbon, 13.0% hydrogen and 34.8% oxygen by mass, and its Mr is 46. Find its empirical and molecular formulae.
questions.model: Step 1: Divide each percentage by its relative atomic mass. C: 52.2 ÷ 12 = 4.35. H: 13.0 ÷ 1 = 13.0. O: 34.8 ÷ 16 = 2.175. Step 2: Divide each by the smallest value, 2.175. C: 4.35 ÷ 2.175 = 2.0. H: 13.0 ÷ 2.175 = 5.98, which is 6. O: 2.175 ÷ 2.175 = 1. The ratio C : H : O is 2 : 6 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₂H₆O. Step 3: The mass of the empirical formula unit is 2(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 46. Step 4: Mr ÷ empirical mass = 46 ÷ 46 = 1, so the molecular formula is the same as the empirical formula: C₂H₆O.

questions.prompt: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in washing soda, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (Na = 23).
questions.model: Step 1: Mr of Na₂CO₃·10H₂O = 2(23) + 12 + 3(16) + 10(18) = 46 + 12 + 48 + 180 = 286. Step 2: Mass of water = 10 × 18 = 180. Step 3: Percentage of water = 180 ÷ 286 × 100 = 62.9%.

questions.prompt: Balance the following equations: (i) C₄H₁₀ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, (ii) Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃, (iii) Ca(OH)₂ + HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.
questions.model: (i) Carbon: 4 atoms on the left, so 4 CO₂ on the right. Hydrogen: 10 atoms on the left, so 5 H₂O on the right. Oxygen: 8 + 5 = 13 atoms on the right, so 13/2 O₂ on the left. Doubling every coefficient gives 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. Check: C 8 = 8, H 20 = 20, O 26 = 26. (ii) Iron and chlorine: 2 Fe on the left needs 2 FeCl₃, which holds 6 Cl, so 3 Cl₂ on the left. Balanced equation: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. Check: Fe 2 = 2, Cl 6 = 6. (iii) Calcium: 1 on each side. Nitrate: 2 NO₃⁻ on the right, so 2HNO₃ on the left. Hydrogen: 2 + 2 = 4 on the left, so 2H₂O on the right. Balanced equation: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O. Check: O 8 = 8, H 4 = 4, N 2 = 2.

questions.prompt: Explain why a chemical equation must be balanced, and state what the coefficients in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O tell you.
questions.model: A chemical equation must be balanced because atoms are conserved in a reaction, in line with the law of conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged to form the products but are not created or destroyed, so the same number of each kind of atom must appear on both sides. The coefficients give the mole ratio of the reaction: 2 mol of hydrogen react with 1 mol of oxygen to give 2 mol of water.
